title: What are temporary tables (`CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE`, session-scoped, auto-dropped), when do you use them (staging intermediate results in complex multi-step queries or ETL), and how do they differ from CTEs — a CTE is a named subquery scoped to one statement and usually inlined by the optimizer, while a temp table persists across statements in the session?

s1_definition.profdef: A temporary table, created with `CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE`, is a real table that exists only for the duration of your database session (or transaction) and is automatically dropped when the session ends. It is used to stage intermediate results across multiple statements in a complex multi-step query or ETL pipeline. A Common Table Expression (CTE), written with `WITH name AS (...)`, is a named subquery scoped to a single statement; the optimizer usually inlines it, so it does not persist and cannot be referenced by later statements. The core difference is lifetime and scope: a temp table lives across statements in the session, a CTE lives only within one statement.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose National Bank of India's month-end ETL has several steps that all need the same filtered set of this month's high-value transactions. A CTE is like writing that filter as a note inside one single instruction — the clerk reads the note while doing that one instruction and then throws it away. A temporary table is like the clerk copying those transactions onto a scratch pad that stays on the desk all shift, so every later instruction in the pipeline can reuse the same scratch pad without re-deriving it.
s1_definition.oneliner: A CTE is a named subquery scoped to one statement and usually inlined; a temp table is a real, session-lived table you reuse across many statements.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A temporary table, created with `CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE`, is a real table that exists only for the duration of your database session (or transaction) and is automatically dropped when the session ends. It is used to stage intermediate results across multiple statements in a complex multi-step query or ETL pipeline. A Common Table Expression (CTE), written with `WITH name AS (...)`, is a named subquery scoped to a single statement; the optimizer usually inlines it, so it does not persist and cannot be referenced by later statements. The core difference is lifetime and scope: a temp table lives across statements in the session, a CTE lives only within one statement.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Suppose National Bank of India's month-end ETL has several steps that all need the same filtered set of this month's high-value transactions. A CTE is like writing that filter as a note inside one single instruction — the clerk reads the note while doing that one instruction and then throws it away. A temporary table is like the clerk copying those transactions onto a scratch pad that stays on the desk all shift, so every later instruction in the pipeline can reuse the same scratch pad without re-deriving it.

**One line to remember:** A CTE is a named subquery scoped to one statement and usually inlined; a temp table is a real, session-lived table you reuse across many statements.

sections.s2_technical:
A temporary table is a genuine table in a special temporary schema, visible only to the session that created it, and dropped automatically at session end (or transaction end if you use ON COMMIT DROP). You can insert into it, index it, query it repeatedly, and join it across several statements. This makes it ideal for ETL and complex reporting where you compute an expensive intermediate set once, optionally index it, and then reuse it in step after step. Because it is a real table, the optimizer has statistics on it and you can ANALYZE it for good plans.

A CTE is syntactic: WITH name AS (subquery) gives a name to a subquery that you can reference within the same single statement, including recursively. It improves readability and lets you reference the same logical set more than once in one statement. In most modern databases the optimizer inlines a CTE into the main query and optimizes the whole thing together, so it is not materialized by default and it vanishes when the statement finishes.

The practical differences follow from lifetime. A CTE cannot be reused by a later statement because it does not outlive its statement. A temp table can be referenced by every subsequent statement until the session ends. A CTE that is referenced many times within one statement may be recomputed each time unless the optimizer materializes it; a temp table is computed once and physically stored, so repeated reuse never recomputes. A temp table can carry its own indexes; a CTE cannot.

When do you choose each? Use a CTE for readability and for breaking one complex statement into logical steps, especially when the intermediate set is small or used once. Use a temporary table when the same expensive intermediate result is needed by several separate statements, when you want to index the intermediate result, or when the dataset is large enough that materializing once beats recomputing.

The senior nuance is cost: temp tables incur write I/O and catalog overhead to create and drop, and heavy temp-table churn can bloat the temp space, so you do not reach for them when a CTE or a plain subquery would do. Conversely, forcing a giant CTE to be recomputed several times in one statement can be slower than staging it in a temp table once.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem: a month-end reconciliation pipeline needs this month's high-value transactions in several steps — a summary by account, a flagged-for-review list, and an audit extract. Re-deriving the filtered set in every step is wasteful.

Problem 1 — the same expensive filter feeds many steps. We stage the filtered high-value transactions into a temporary table once, so each later step reads the staged data instead of re-scanning the huge source table.

Problem 2 — one step needs only a named subquery. For a single summary statement we show a CTE, which is inlined and scoped to that one statement, demonstrating when a CTE is the right, lighter choice.

Problem 3 — lifetime matters. We show that the temp table is still queryable in a later step, while the CTE is gone after its statement.

The code models a SessionDb that supports a session-scoped temp table and single-statement CTEs, a ReconciliationService that stages a temp table and runs multiple steps against it, and a demo contrasting both.

temp-cte-service/
├── pom.xml
├── src/main/java/com/bank/tempcte/
│   ├── TempCteDemo.java
│   ├── db/SessionDb.java

└── src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_tables.sql

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__create_tables.sql (Flyway)
CREATE TABLE transactions (
    txn_id     BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    account_id VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    amount     DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
);

-- TEMP TABLE: compute the expensive set ONCE, reuse across statements:
-- CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE tmp_high_value ON COMMIT DROP AS
--   SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE amount >= 100000 AND created_at >= date_trunc('month', now());
-- CREATE INDEX ON tmp_high_value(account_id);         -- temp tables can be indexed
-- SELECT account_id, SUM(amount) FROM tmp_high_value GROUP BY account_id;  -- step 1
-- SELECT * FROM tmp_high_value WHERE amount >= 1000000;                     -- step 2 (reuse)

-- CTE: named subquery scoped to ONE statement only:
-- WITH high_value AS (
--   SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE amount >= 100000
-- )
-- SELECT account_id, COUNT(*) FROM high_value GROUP BY account_id;          -- gone after this
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
etl:
  high-value-threshold: 100000
  very-high-threshold: 1000000
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input: four transactions, a high-value threshold of Rs.1,00,000, and a very-high threshold of Rs.10,00,000.

Step 1 — The pipeline creates a temporary table tmp_high_value holding the three transactions at or above Rs.1,00,000. This expensive filter runs once and the result is physically staged for the whole session.

Step 2 — Step 1 of the pipeline reads the temp table and sums by account, producing a per-account summary without re-scanning the source transactions.

Step 3 — Step 2 of the pipeline reads the same temp table again to find transactions at or above Rs.10,00,000 for review. There is no re-derivation of the base set — the staged temp table is reused.

Step 4 — Separately, a one-shot count uses a CTE: the named subquery is inlined into that single statement, produces the count, and is discarded. It cannot be referenced afterward.

Step 5 — The session ends and the temporary table is automatically dropped, freeing its space.

Final output:

```
2026-10-25 17:37:00 [INFO] === Temp table: staged once, reused across steps ===
2026-10-25 17:37:00 [INFO] CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE tmp_high_value (3 rows staged)
2026-10-25 17:37:00 [INFO] Step 1 summary by account: {SAV2001=1350000, CUR3001=300000}
2026-10-25 17:37:00 [INFO] Step 2 flagged for review: 1 txns
2026-10-25 17:37:00 [INFO] === CTE: single-statement, inlined ===
2026-10-25 17:37:00 [INFO] WITH high_value AS (...) — inlined, scoped to this statement only
2026-10-25 17:37:00 [INFO] One-shot CTE count: 3
2026-10-25 17:37:00 [INFO] session ended → temp table auto-dropped
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Month-end ETL session
    │
    ▼
  CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE tmp_high_value AS SELECT ... (expensive filter runs ONCE)
    │  persists for the session, can be indexed
    ├─ Step 1: SELECT account, SUM(amount) FROM tmp_high_value       (reuse)
    └─ Step 2: SELECT * FROM tmp_high_value WHERE amount>=10,00,000   (reuse, no re-scan)
    │
    ▼  (separately)
  WITH high_value AS (SELECT ...) SELECT COUNT(*) FROM high_value     (inlined, one statement)
    │  vanishes after the statement
    ▼
  session end → tmp_high_value auto-dropped
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Temp Table vs CTE ═══

  ┌─ Patterns ────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Staging: materialize once, reuse many (temp table)        │
  │  Inline subquery: readability, single-statement (CTE)      │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ┌─ SOLID ───────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: SessionDb owns storage/lifetime; Service owns steps.   │
  │  O: new pipeline step = new method, temp table unchanged.  │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────┐        ┌───────────────────────┐
  │ ReconciliationService    │───────▶│ SessionDb             │
  │ + runPipeline(db,...)    │ uses   │ - transactions: List  │
  │ + oneShotCount(db,...)   │        │ - tempHighValue: List │ ← session-scoped
  └──────────────────────────┘        │ + createTempHighValue │
                                       │ + tempTable()         │
                                       │ + cteHighValue()      │ ← statement-scoped
                                       │ + endSession()        │
                                       └───────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. createTempHighValue(100000)  → stage 3 rows (persists)
  2. tempTable() → summary        (reuse)
  3. tempTable() → flagged        (reuse, no re-scan)
  4. cteHighValue(100000)         → inlined, discarded
  5. endSession()                 → temp table dropped
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A temporary table, created with CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE, is a genuine table that lives only for the duration of my database session, or just the transaction if I use ON COMMIT DROP, and it is automatically dropped when the session ends. Because it is a real table, I can insert into it, index it, gather statistics on it, and query it repeatedly across many separate statements. That makes it the right tool for complex multi-step queries and ETL pipelines, where I compute an expensive intermediate result once, optionally index it, and then reuse it in step after step without re-deriving it.

A Common Table Expression, written with WITH name AS a subquery, is a named subquery scoped to a single statement. It makes a complex statement readable and lets me reference the same logical set more than once within that one statement, and in modern databases the optimizer usually inlines it rather than materializing it. The crucial difference is lifetime and scope: a CTE disappears when its statement finishes and cannot be referenced by any later statement, while a temporary table persists across every statement in the session. A CTE cannot carry its own index; a temp table can. A CTE referenced several times in one statement may be recomputed each time, whereas a temp table is stored once and never recomputed.

In our National Bank of India month-end reconciliation, the pipeline needed this month's high-value transactions for a per-account summary, a flagged-for-review list, and an audit extract. I staged that expensive filter into a temporary table once and indexed it, then every step read the staged data instead of re-scanning the two-hundred-million-row source, which cut the job time dramatically. For a single one-off count in another report, a CTE was the lighter and correct choice because the set was used once inside one statement. The rule I state is that a CTE is a named subquery scoped to one statement and usually inlined, while a temp table is a real, session-lived table I reuse across many statements — so I pick a CTE for readability and single-statement logic, and a temp table when the same expensive intermediate is needed by several statements or deserves its own index.

---

keyPoints: Correlated subquery: references outer query — runs per row
CTE (WITH clause): named temporary result set
Recursive CTE: hierarchical queries (org chart, tree structures)
